survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports PISA 2022 results for Estonia using the OECD PISA 2022 Database. The note describes that PISA uses complex sampling and that some countries/economies may have caution flags when sampling standards are not met; for Estonia, the note states that all data met PISA quality standards. The factsheet reports proficiency levels and mean performance comparisons (including uncertainty via 95% confidence intervals), which in PISA are typically based on the survey design and scaling procedures used in the OECD database. Because this is a descriptive results factsheet (not an original micro-data modeling study), the manuscript does not specify whether analysts applied student/sampling weights or replicate weights in a custom way; users should rely on the OECD PISA 2022 database’s standard weighted estimation procedures for any re-analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive OECD PISA 2022 results factsheet rather than an empirical student-level analysis paper. It reports proficiency shares and mean performance estimates sourced from the OECD PISA 2022 Database tables, without specifying an analysis pipeline that would require the authors to document plausible-value (PV) handling or missing-data procedures. Therefore, PV and missing-data handling are not reported at the level of this factsheet, because the underlying OECD scaling/estimation methodology is encapsulated in the database products rather than re-estimated here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The factsheet reports that, in Estonia, 6,392 students in 196 schools completed the assessment in mathematics, reading, or science in PISA 2022. No additional analytic filtering (e.g., exclusions by missing background variables or specific subdomains) is described in the factsheet; it presents the standard PISA 2022 reporting population for Estonia.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Estonia factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in Estonia performed in mathematics, reading, and science, and how performance relates to student background and school experiences. PISA 2022 used two two-hour subject tests with different booklets and a background questionnaire (about 35 minutes), and the factsheet reports mean performance trends, proficiency-level distributions (e.g., Level 2 baseline and Levels 5–6 top performers), and within-country gaps by socio-economic status and gender. For Estonia, the note states that all data met PISA quality standards, so estimates are presented without the caution flag used when sampling standards are not reached. The factsheet also highlights COVID-related learning disruptions and school climate indicators, but it does not provide an original predictive modeling approach or model performance metrics. As a result, the document is best interpreted as descriptive evidence for benchmarking and diagnostic discussion rather than as a causal or ML-based evaluation.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical ML paper and does not report an analysis design, PV/missing-data handling choices, or any trained predictive models; it is a descriptive results factsheet drawing on OECD’s PISA 2022 Database tables. Consequently, fields such as main_findings (structured ML outcomes), confounders, and ML techniques are intentionally empty because no student-level predictive modeling is conducted or evaluated in the text provided. The factsheet’s role is to communicate benchmarks (means, trends, and proficiency shares) and contextual indicators for Estonia rather than to estimate new statistical relationships.
